s: Discovery data shows that a company's order management application makes thousands of low-latency calls per minute to an on-premises Oracle database that also serves the company's inventory and billing applications. Several small internal web applications have no dependencies on other systems. The company has a 10 Gbps AWS Direct Connect connection with 12 ms of latency to AWS, and the migration team is new to AWS. The company must avoid performance degradation during the migration. How should the migration waves be planned?
o: Migrate the independent internal web applications first as pilot waves to build skills. Then migrate the order management, inventory, and billing applications together with the shared Oracle database in the same wave.
Migrate the order management application first because it is the most critical, and keep the shared database on premises until all dependent applications have moved.
Migrate the shared Oracle database first, and then move each dependent application in separate later waves.
Migrate all applications, including the pilot candidates, in a single wave to avoid any hybrid latency.

w.y: Independent, low-risk applications are good pilot waves for building skills. Tightly coupled, chatty applications and their shared database should move together in one wave so that no high-volume calls cross the 12 ms hybrid link, which avoids performance degradation.

o.A: Correct: low-risk pilots first, then the dependency group as one move group.
o.B: Thousands of calls per minute across 12 ms of latency would degrade performance, and starting with the most critical application is high risk.
o.C: The applications left on premises would call the database across the hybrid link and degrade.
o.D: A big-bang migration by an inexperienced team carries high risk and offers no chance to learn first.

d: avoid performance degradation; migration team is new to AWS
